title: Fire and the blade of grass
hookLine: the gods win a victory and take the credit; then a stranger appears
carry: every power is lent by brahman
last: UNKNOWN TO THOSE WHO CLAIM IT.

cards: The locker room after a championship is loud. Everyone's giving interviews. I made that shot.
My defense won it. Nobody mentions the coach, or the thousand things that had to go right. After two sections of paradox, the Kena changes gear and tells a story.
It starts in a locker room, more or less: the gods have just won a great victory, and they're very pleased with themselves.

teach.b: Section three. Brahman won a victory for the gods. The text doesn't say against whom; tradition says the asuras, the gods' old rivals.
But the gods felt great in that victory, and said: this victory is ours, this greatness is ours. You can hear it. Ours.
Brahman knew what they were thinking, and appeared before them. Not as a voice from heaven.
As a yaksha: a wondrous, mysterious being they couldn't place. So they turned to Agni, the god of fire, the one who knows all beings. Agni, find out what this wondrous being is.
Agni ran up to it. Who are you? I am Agni, the one who knows all beings.
And what power is in you?

teach.h: I COULD BURN THE WHOLE EARTH.
teach.b: I could burn up everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this.
Agni rushed at it with all his speed, and couldn't burn it. He went back to the gods: I couldn't find out what this being is. That's the heart of the story.

teach.h: FIRE CANNOT BURN ONE BLADE OF GRASS.
teach.b: Fire, who can burn the world, can't burn a blade of grass. Why? Go back to the teaching: the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind.
On that pattern, Brahman is the one by which fire burns. Agni's power was never his own. It was on loan.

When the one it came from simply held it back, there was nothing left. That's the teaching under a custom many Hindu families keep: a first paycheck, a report card, a trophy goes before the home shrine first.

teach.h: EVERY POWER IS LENT BY BRAHMAN.
teach.b: To say: this power was lent.

how: The Kena's story of Agni and the blade of grass is retold in Hindu teaching and children's storybooks as a lesson that every power comes from Brahman. Many families also set a first paycheck, exam results or a prize before the home shrine as thanks.

a wondrous being no one can place
a demon sent to test the gods

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: a wondrous being they couldn't place
claimed he could burn the whole earth

s: the gods won the victory by their own power
the text says Brahman won it for them; they took the credit.
Agni couldn't burn a single blade of grass
the god of fire rushed at it with all his speed and failed.
the Kena names who the gods were fighting
the text doesn't say; tradition says the asuras.

games.q: you're Agni, god of fire. a stranger sets down one blade of grass and says: burn this. what happens?
o: you can't burn it, no matter how hard you try.
games.why: Agni rushed at it with all his speed and couldn't burn it. his power had never been his own.

practice: Think of something you're proud of, a skill, a win, a talent, and let yourself feel good about it. Then, if you pray, set it, or something that stands for it, before your shrine, or simply bow and say: this was given.
If you don't, list what it rested on: your body working, the people who taught you, the breath you didn't earn. Let the pride stay, and let it widen into thanks.

wordCard.voice: Yaksha, a wondrous or mysterious being. Brahman won the gods' victory, but they said, this is ours; Brahman appeared before them as a yaksha, and fire could not burn a single blade of grass.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yaksha, a wondrous or mysterious being; the form Brahman takes before the proud gods.

carryVoice: Your line: every power is lent by brahman. Even fire's power was on loan. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Kena Upanishad 3.1–3.6 (the gods' victory; the yaksha; Agni and the blade of grass)
